paragraphs: This paper studies convex optimization problems with affine constraints and a compact domain, a setting that includes important semidefinite programming applications. The challenge is to find solutions that both improve the objective and satisfy the constraints. Existing conditional gradient methods either do not cover this combination of requirements or can be slow in practice.

The proposed method combines smoothing with an augmented Lagrangian framework in a unified approach. It retains two useful features of classical conditional gradient methods: inexpensive calls to a linear minimization oracle and a sparse representation of the decision variable. These features matter because handling constraints should not require abandoning the computational advantages that made conditional gradients attractive.

The authors prove an O(1/√k) convergence rate for both objective residual and feasibility gap. Thus, the analysis tracks progress toward a good objective value and toward constraint satisfaction together. The theoretical rate essentially matches existing methods for this problem setting, while the paper argues for better practical performance across several applications.
icml-2019-a-conditional-gradient-based-a.tldr: A conditional gradient method combines smoothing and augmented Lagrangian ideas while preserving inexpensive updates and proving convergence in objective value and constraint satisfaction.

paragraphs: Federated learning addresses situations where data lives on separate servers and cannot easily be collected in one place. This paper asks how to build a global neural network from knowledge already represented in local networks. Its starting assumption is that each server supplies its neural network weights, giving the central learning procedure model information without pooling the underlying data.

The authors develop a Bayesian nonparametric framework for modeling those local weights and an inference procedure for synthesizing a more expressive global network. The synthesis requires no additional supervision and can operate with as few as one communication round. This makes communication requirements part of the contribution alongside the statistical approach to combining local models.

The paper demonstrates the approach on federated learning settings simulated from two image classification datasets. These experiments support the usefulness of constructing a shared model from local weights. The stated result is a way to combine distributed neural networks while avoiding data pooling, with the possibility of very limited communication.
icml-2019-bayesian-nonparametric-federat.tldr: A Bayesian framework combines local neural network weights into a more expressive global network without pooling data, potentially using one communication round.

paragraphs: Circuit-GNN tackles the slow process of designing distributed circuits, where engineers repeatedly simulate electromagnetic behavior and adjust a design. The model learns to predict those electromagnetic properties, allowing it to serve in place of a traditional simulator. Its graph neural network structure lets a single model work across different circuit topologies.

The same model also supports the inverse task: starting from desired electromagnetic specifications and finding a circuit that meets them. Because the neural network is differentiable, gradients can guide changes to circuit parameters and topology. Simulation and design therefore become connected parts of the approach, with the learned predictor providing a route for optimizing the circuit itself.

Against a commercial simulator, the paper reports a reduction in simulation time of four orders of magnitude. It also demonstrates a Terahertz channelizer with performance comparable to a manually optimized design, potentially saving weeks of expert optimization. The model produces designs beyond commonly used templates, showing how the approach can expand the explored design space.
icml-2019-circuit-gnn-graph-neural-netwo.tldr: Circuit-GNN learns fast electromagnetic simulation and uses gradients to optimize circuit parameters and topology, including designs beyond standard templates.

paragraphs: This paper develops stochastic conditional gradient methods that use variance reduction to improve optimization efficiency. Its central construction combines the classical Frank–Wolfe method with SPIDER, a stochastic path-integrated differential estimator. The resulting method, SPIDER-FW, connects the choice of gradient estimator to the complexity guarantees of a conditional gradient algorithm.

The framework covers two objective types: finite sums and more general expectations. A finite-sum objective aggregates a collection of terms, while an expectation objective expresses an average over a distribution. Addressing both settings broadens the scope of the proposed method beyond problems described by a fixed collection of terms. The paper also extends the framework using conditional gradient sliding, producing a second method called SPIDER-CGS.

The main stated findings concern theoretical complexity. In nonconvex optimization, SPIDER-FW has stronger complexity guarantees, while in the convex setting it matches the best known Frank–Wolfe variants. The distinction matters: the contribution claims an improvement for the nonconvex case and competitive guarantees for the convex case.
icml-2019-conditional-gradient-methods-v.tldr: SPIDER-based variance reduction strengthens nonconvex conditional gradient complexity guarantees while matching leading Frank–Wolfe variants in the convex setting.

paragraphs: Zero-shot object recognition uses auxiliary semantic knowledge to classify objects without relying on labeled examples of every target category. This paper focuses on a source of evidence that earlier approaches overlooked: the context surrounding an object. An object's own appearance provides useful information, but the other objects in the image can also help establish what it is likely to be.

The authors propose context-aware zero-shot learning, using semantic representations to model how likely an object is to occur in a particular context. This changes the role of semantic information from describing the object alone to helping describe its relationship with its surroundings. The approach follows the observation that objects occur more naturally in some contexts than in others.

Experiments on Visual Genome show that contextual information can substantially improve standard zero-shot recognition. The paper also reports robustness to class imbalance, where categories have unequal representation. These findings support treating surrounding objects as useful recognition evidence, alongside the intrinsic properties of the object being classified.
icml-2019-context-aware-zero-shot-learni.tldr: Modeling which objects fit a scene's context substantially improves zero-shot recognition in the reported Visual Genome experiments.

paragraphs: Learning a directed acyclic graph from observed samples is difficult because the number of possible graphs grows extremely quickly. Earlier work made this search amenable to continuous optimization by imposing a constraint that rules out directed cycles. DAG-GNN builds on that idea while moving beyond a linear structural equation model and its least-squares formulation.

The proposed approach uses a deep generative model centered on a variational autoencoder with a graph neural network architecture. A variant of the acyclicity constraint guides learning of the graph structure. The richer neural model is intended to capture nonlinear relationships, and it naturally accommodates discrete variables and variables represented by vectors.

On synthetic data generated through nonlinear relationships, the method learns more accurate graphs. On benchmark datasets containing discrete variables, its learned graphs are reasonably close to global optima. These results support combining continuous graph optimization with a more expressive model, while the reported closeness to an optimum remains an empirical finding rather than a guarantee of exact graph recovery.
icml-2019-dag-gnn-dag-structure-learning.tldr: DAG-GNN combines a graph-based variational autoencoder with an acyclicity constraint to learn graph structures involving nonlinear, discrete, or vector-valued variables.

paragraphs: This paper studies optimization algorithms by connecting their iterative behavior to continuous dynamical systems. The focus is the alternating direction method of multipliers, or ADMM, which is widely used in machine learning and statistics. Much previous work on this connection considered smooth objectives, leaving out nonsmooth problems that are important applications of ADMM.

The authors use differential inclusions to analyze nonsmooth versions of several established algorithms: linearized ADMM, gradient-based ADMM, generalized ADMM, and accelerated generalized ADMM. Differential inclusions provide the continuous-system language for this analysis. The contribution is to investigate convergence behavior and establish connections between these discrete optimization methods and corresponding dynamical descriptions.

This perspective matters because it extends the continuous-limit study of ADMM beyond objectives covered by smooth analyses. It brings multiple widely used variants into a framework suited to nonsmooth problems. The authors anticipate that these connections will offer new understanding of ADMM; the stated contribution centers on analysis and interpretation of existing methods rather than an empirical performance improvement.
icml-2019-differential-inclusions-for-mo.tldr: Differential inclusions connect several nonsmooth ADMM variants to continuous dynamical systems and support analysis of their convergence behavior.

paragraphs: Dirichlet Simplex Nest is a family of probabilistic models designed to accommodate different kinds of data. The paper develops inference algorithms that take advantage of the models' geometry, particularly their convex structure and low-dimensional simplicial organization. The central idea is that this structure can guide learning, making geometric properties a source of computational and statistical benefits.

The inference approach uses a connection to Voronoi tessellation together with properties of the Dirichlet distribution. These ingredients support algorithms described as both fast and provably accurate. For a range of model settings and data distributions, the authors establish consistency and strong error bounds, giving theoretical support for the accuracy of the inferred model as well as its computational appeal.

The paper demonstrates the model and learning procedure through simulations and analyses of text and financial data. These examples illustrate applicability across different data domains. The combined contribution is a probabilistic model class and a geometrically informed inference method, with guarantees that apply across the stated range of settings.
icml-2019-dirichlet-simplex-nest-and-geo.tldr: Dirichlet Simplex Nest uses low-dimensional convex geometry to enable fast inference with consistency and error guarantees across a range of settings.

paragraphs: Distributed learning systems commonly expect exchanged gradients or models to arrive reliably. This paper asks whether training can tolerate a network that sometimes drops those messages. It studies a parameter-server architecture in which each worker–server communication has a nonzero probability of being lost, making the pattern of successful connections vary during training.

The authors analyze this situation as distributed learning over random topologies. Their theoretical result shows that such learning can achieve convergence rates comparable to centralized training or distributed training over reliable networks. They also prove that the influence of packet loss decreases as the number of parameter servers increases, linking the effect of unreliability to the system's architecture.

The paper connects the theory to training deep neural networks over an unreliable network layer and uses network simulation to validate system improvements. The significance is that reliable delivery need not be taken as an unquestioned prerequisite for the studied training setup. The result supports designing learning and communication together so that training can tolerate some dropped exchanges.
icml-2019-distributed-learning-over-unre.tldr: Distributed training can retain comparable convergence rates despite dropped messages, with packet-loss effects diminishing as the number of parameter servers grows.

paragraphs: This paper develops a generative model that represents scenes as compositions of objects while explicitly accounting for occlusion. Overlapping objects make scene interpretation difficult because visible pixels do not reveal every object equally. The model addresses this by separating each object's latent representation into location, size, shape, and appearance, rather than treating the scene only as an undivided image.

Scene generation combines these object representations with an infinite-dimensional binary vector indicating which objects are present. Training is unsupervised and learns spatial dependencies among pixels. Inference over the latent variables can then estimate the number of objects, separate their pixels, and identify object presence in regions where objects overlap.

The authors evaluate the approach on specially designed datasets and report better performance than two leading methods when occlusions are present. These findings support explicitly incorporating overlap into an object-based generative model. The contribution connects image generation with several aspects of scene understanding through the same latent representation, including object counting and pixel-level separation.
icml-2019-generative-modeling-of-infinit.tldr: An unsupervised object-based generative model explicitly handles occlusion to infer object counts, pixel assignments, and presence in overlapping regions.

paragraphs: Block coordinate descent methods have shown practical promise for training deep neural networks, but their theoretical behavior is harder to establish because training is highly nonconvex. This paper develops a general methodology for proving convergence of these methods. It seeks to explain whether the iterative training process approaches a critical point under the covered formulations.

For most commonly used training models involving two-splitting and three-splitting schemes, the authors establish global convergence to a critical point with an O(1/k) rate, where k counts iterations. A critical point is the target of the result; the claim does not establish convergence to a globally optimal neural network. This distinction is essential when interpreting convergence language in nonconvex optimization.

The analysis extends to general losses with Lipschitz continuous gradients and to deep residual networks. Its technical foundation adds new elements to the Kurdyka–Łojasiewicz inequality framework. Together, these results provide a broader theoretical basis for block coordinate descent in deep learning, connecting practical training methods with provable convergence behavior.
icml-2019-global-convergence-of-block-co.tldr: The paper establishes O(1/k) convergence to a critical point for broad classes of block coordinate descent methods used in deep learning.

paragraphs: Training with corrupted labels requires deciding which examples to trust. Co-teaching addresses this by training two neural networks that select low-loss examples for each other. The paper identifies a problem with that arrangement: as training progresses, the networks can come to agree, reducing the distinction between the two learners and making the procedure resemble self-training.

Co-teaching+ adds a disagreement filter before selecting training examples. Both networks first predict on the data, and only examples on which their predictions differ are retained. Each network then chooses low-loss examples from that subset. For its parameter update, each network uses the examples selected by its peer, preserving the cross-training structure of the original approach.

This combination focuses updates on examples where the learners still differ while retaining the small-loss selection mechanism for handling noisy labels. Benchmark experiments show substantially greater robustness than many leading methods. The findings support disagreement as a useful component of this training procedure, with the reported advantage grounded in empirical evaluation of the resulting models.
icml-2019-how-does-disagreement-help-gen.tldr: Co-teaching+ trains two networks on peer-selected, low-loss examples where they disagree, improving robustness to noisy labels in benchmark experiments.

paragraphs: Visual recognition often requires relating features that lie far apart in an image. A fully connected graph neural network can represent these nonlocal relationships, but computing a dense matrix of affinities between features makes that strategy difficult to scale. LatentGNN addresses this computational obstacle while retaining the ability to represent context beyond nearby image regions.

The key idea is to introduce a latent space that reduces the complexity of the graph. This enables a low-rank representation of the affinity matrix and gives linear computational complexity. Instead of requiring the full dense representation, the method uses the latent structure to build an efficient and flexible account of relationships among visual features.

The paper evaluates the approach on three major visual recognition tasks and reports substantial improvements over prior work while maintaining low computational cost. These findings connect the representational goal with the efficiency goal: modeling long-range context can improve recognition without carrying the cost of the dense graph formulation considered in the paper.
icml-2019-latentgnn-learning-efficient-n.tldr: LatentGNN uses a latent, low-rank graph representation to capture long-range visual relationships with linear computational complexity.

paragraphs: Generative image models can struggle with structure that must remain consistent across a whole image. A building's regularly spaced windows illustrate the problem: producing individual windows is only part of the task, because their overall arrangement also matters. This paper addresses that difficulty by incorporating programs that explicitly represent global structure into a generative model.

The programs provide a way to describe repeated spatial organization. For example, a two-dimensional loop can represent a repeating arrangement of windows. The authors also introduce a learning framework that uses program synthesis to obtain training data for these models. The approach therefore connects a structured description of the image with a procedure for learning to generate it.

On synthetic and real-world data, the paper reports substantial improvements over leading methods in both image generation and image completion when global structure is involved. These findings suggest that representing regularity explicitly can help a model coordinate different image regions. The benefit applies to creating structured images and to filling in missing portions of them.
icml-2019-learning-neurosymbolic-generat.tldr: Programs that represent global image structure, learned using program-synthesized training data, improve generation and completion of structured images.

paragraphs: A small shift in an input image can cause a large change in a convolutional network's output. This paper connects that instability to common downsampling operations, including pooling and strided convolutions, that overlook the sampling theorem. It revisits the signal-processing remedy of applying a low-pass filter before reducing spatial resolution.

The central issue is how to integrate this anti-aliasing step into a neural network. Simply inserting a filtering module can hurt performance. The paper shows that a suitable integration is compatible with existing components such as max-pooling, and that the technique can be used across layer types and applications, including image classification and conditional image generation.

The reported results show increased shift-invariance and improved ImageNet classification accuracy across several commonly used architectures. The authors interpret the accuracy gains as evidence that anti-aliasing provides effective regularization. The contribution is therefore both greater stability under image translations and an observed improvement in predictive performance through a carefully incorporated classical signal-processing technique.
icml-2019-making-convolutional-networks-.tldr: Properly integrated anti-aliasing makes convolutional networks more stable under image shifts and improves ImageNet accuracy across several tested architectures.

paragraphs: Poorly specified rewards can lead reinforcement learning agents toward unwanted behavior. Choosing suitable rewards becomes especially difficult when multiple agents interact, because the meaning of rational behavior is more complicated. This paper develops MA-AIRL, a framework for learning reward functions from expert demonstrations in multi-agent settings rather than specifying all those rewards by hand.

The method targets Markov games with high-dimensional state and action spaces and unknown dynamics. Its derivation combines a new solution concept with maximum pseudolikelihood estimation inside an adversarial reward-learning framework. These components provide a way to formulate and estimate rewards while accounting for the interacting-agent setting that makes a direct extension of inverse reinforcement learning difficult.

In experiments, MA-AIRL recovers rewards that are highly correlated with the ground-truth rewards and substantially improves policy imitation over prior methods. These are complementary findings: one concerns agreement with the underlying reward signal, and the other concerns reproducing demonstrated behavior. Together, they support the framework's usefulness for multi-agent reward learning and imitation.
icml-2019-multi-agent-adversarial-invers.tldr: MA-AIRL learns rewards from multi-agent demonstrations, recovering highly correlated reward functions and improving policy imitation in the reported experiments.

paragraphs: Neural Collaborative Subspace Clustering groups data assumed to come from a union of low-dimensional subspaces. The goal is to discover which points belong together according to that underlying structure. The proposed neural model operates without a spectral clustering stage, a design choice the authors connect to its ability to scale to large datasets.

At the center of the method is a classifier that judges whether two points lie in the same subspace. Training uses two affinity matrices, which represent relationships between points. One matrix comes from the classifier; the other comes from subspace self-expressiveness. The two sources supervise learning collaboratively, linking pairwise predictions with information derived from the subspace structure.

The paper assesses the model against a range of leading clustering methods, including deep subspace-based approaches. The abstract describes this comparative evaluation without asserting a specific performance advantage. Its main stated contribution is the collaborative neural formulation: it combines two relationship representations to learn clusters while removing the need for spectral clustering.
icml-2019-neural-collaborative-subspace-.tldr: A neural clustering model jointly learns from pairwise classification and subspace affinities without requiring spectral clustering.

paragraphs: Parallel stochastic gradient descent has two distinct costs: computing stochastic gradients and exchanging information between workers. Classical data-parallel SGD can gain linear speedup from N workers, but it communicates after every batch. This paper studies whether increasing batch sizes during training can preserve strong convergence guarantees while reducing the number of communication rounds.

For stochastic nonconvex objectives satisfying the P-L condition, the authors analyze classical parallel SGD with exponentially increasing batches. They establish an O(1/(NT)) convergence rate with linear speedup and only log(T) communication rounds. The P-L condition is a substantive qualification: this stronger rate is tied to that particular class of optimization problems.

For general stochastic nonconvex optimization, the paper proposes a Catalyst-like algorithm with an O(1/√(NT)) convergence rate and O(√(NT) log(T/N)) communication rounds. Both convergence rates are described as the fastest known for their respective settings. The contribution shows how batch scheduling and algorithm design can reduce communication while retaining strong computational convergence guarantees.
icml-2019-on-the-computation-and-communi.tldr: Increasing batch sizes enables parallel SGD methods to retain strong nonconvex convergence rates with substantially fewer communication rounds.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization aims to make training faster by spreading computation across multiple machines. That benefit can be undermined by communication overhead, which is often a bottleneck. Previous analyses had established linear speedup for distributed SGD variants with reduced communication, leaving open whether a distributed method using momentum could enjoy the same combination of properties.

The paper studies a communication-efficient momentum SGD method for nonconvex optimization and proves its linear speedup property. This addresses the theoretical question of whether adding computing nodes can scale the method's optimization progress favorably while retaining its communication-efficient design. The focus is the analyzed method, rather than an assertion about every distributed momentum algorithm.

The result matters because momentum is widely used in practical machine learning, where it can often improve convergence and generalization. Those practical motivations make a theoretical account of distributed momentum valuable. The paper's stated contribution supplies that account for linear speedup, connecting a commonly used optimization ingredient with the scaling guarantees sought in distributed training.
icml-2019-on-the-linear-speedup-analysis.tldr: The paper proves linear speedup for a communication-efficient distributed momentum SGD method in nonconvex optimization.

paragraphs: This paper studies online principal component analysis and variance minimization when the environment changes over time. A common way to evaluate online algorithms is static regret, which compares their accumulated performance with the best single fixed action chosen in hindsight. That comparison can be poorly suited to a setting where what works well changes during the sequence.

The authors instead use adaptive regret and develop algorithms for both PCA and variance minimization with sublinear adaptive regret guarantees. The shift in evaluation is central to the work: the algorithms are analyzed through a criterion intended to reflect changing conditions, rather than relying only on comparison with one fixed choice for the entire history.

The paper provides both theoretical and experimental evidence that the proposed algorithms can adapt to changing environments. These findings connect the performance criterion to the intended behavior of the methods. The contribution is a combination of adaptive algorithms and guarantees that better address the changing-environment setting motivating the study.
icml-2019-online-adaptive-principal-comp.tldr: Online PCA and variance-minimization algorithms use adaptive regret guarantees to address environments that change over time.

paragraphs: Self-Attention Generative Adversarial Networks address the difficulty of coordinating distant parts of a generated image. Traditional convolutional GANs generate fine details from spatially local information in lower-resolution features. SAGAN adds self-attention so that a detail can draw on cues from all feature locations, allowing image generation to account more directly for long-range relationships.

The discriminator also benefits from this broader view: it can assess whether detailed features in distant image regions agree with one another. Separately, the authors apply spectral normalization to the generator and find improved training dynamics. The approach therefore addresses both spatial coordination in generated images and the behavior of the adversarial training process.

On ImageNet, the paper reports an Inception score increase from 36.8 to 52.52 and a Fréchet Inception distance decrease from 27.62 to 18.65 relative to the best published results cited. Attention visualizations show neighborhoods corresponding to object shapes, supporting the interpretation that the generator uses image-dependent relationships beyond fixed local regions.
icml-2019-self-attention-generative-adve.tldr: SAGAN combines long-range self-attention with generator spectral normalization to improve image generation and training dynamics.

paragraphs: Worst-case reinforcement learning bounds can be much more pessimistic than practical performance. This paper seeks guarantees that reflect features of the particular environment, helping explain why some learning problems are easier than the worst case suggests. It develops an algorithm and analysis for discrete Markov decision processes with a finite horizon.

The algorithm achieves leading worst-case regret bounds while also obtaining substantially tighter bounds when the environment has special features. It does so without requiring advance knowledge of those features. This combination matters because an algorithm can retain a strong general guarantee while benefiting, in its analysis, from favorable problem structure that was not supplied beforehand.

The analysis also contributes to an open question about episodic processes whose total reward has a constant upper bound. Under that condition, the paper gives a regret bound expressed in the number of episodes with no horizon dependence. This specific result demonstrates how a stated structural condition can yield a more informative guarantee than a general worst-case analysis.
icml-2019-tighter-problem-dependent-regr.tldr: A reinforcement learning algorithm retains strong worst-case regret guarantees while obtaining tighter bounds from favorable environment structure without prior domain knowledge.

paragraphs: The trimmed ℓ1 penalty changes sparse estimation by leaving the h largest parameter entries unpenalized. This paper studies how that choice affects statistical behavior, addressing a gap left by earlier optimization-focused work. Its analysis covers recovery of the nonzero parameter locations and estimation errors measured in the ℓ∞ and ℓ2 norms.

The results distinguish regimes according to how h compares with the true number of nonzero parameters. This makes the trimming parameter central to understanding the estimator. The authors also introduce an optimization algorithm with the same theoretical convergence rate as difference-of-convex algorithms, while reporting faster practical execution and lower attained objective values.

Experiments in sparse linear regression and graphical model estimation indicate that trimming can outperform ordinary ℓ1 regularization and nonconvex alternatives. The paper additionally reports promising results for recovering input structure and sparsifying deep networks. Together, the contributions connect statistical analysis, an optimization procedure, and applications, while treating the empirical advantages as possibilities demonstrated in the evaluated settings.
icml-2019-trimming-the-ell-1-regularizer.tldr: The paper analyzes trimmed ℓ1 regularization, develops a practical optimizer, and reports benefits for sparse estimation and two deep learning tasks.

paragraphs: This paper asks how a learner can use both fully labeled supervised data and contextual bandit feedback. The motivation is to benefit from an existing source of supervision while also learning from bandit data. A central complication is that the underlying learning signals in the two sources may differ, so their combination must account for possible disagreement.

The authors develop and prove no-regret algorithms that are robust to divergences between those signals. Robustness to the mismatch is part of the theoretical objective, rather than assuming that the two sources provide interchangeable information. The resulting framework addresses whether supervised information can help initialize or support bandit learning even when the sources do not align.

The paper evaluates some of its algorithms on a large collection of datasets and finds the approaches feasible and helpful in practice. The theoretical and empirical contributions play complementary roles: the guarantees address divergence between sources, while the experiments support the practical usefulness of combining the two forms of feedback.
icml-2019-warm-starting-contextual-bandi.tldr: No-regret algorithms combine supervised and contextual bandit data while remaining robust to differences in their learning signals.

paragraphs: Standard classification often assumes the decision-maker can access all relevant samples. This paper considers situations where access is indirect or inspection capacity is limited. The decision-maker, called the principal, must rely on another party, called the agent, either to supply samples or to identify which samples deserve attention.

The difficulty arises when the agent's objective differs from the principal's. In that case, the selected evidence may reflect what benefits the agent rather than what represents the available information. The principal therefore needs a decision policy that accounts for the agent's incentives. Sample selection becomes part of the decision problem itself, rather than a neutral step that happens before classification.

The paper introduces a theoretical framework for this setting and establishes structural and computational results. Its contribution is to make strategic control over evidence an explicit object of analysis. This framing matters whenever a decision depends on samples chosen by someone with a potentially different goal, because the policy must consider how those samples are selected.
icml-2019-when-samples-are-strategically.tldr: A theoretical framework studies classification when another party strategically selects the samples shown to the decision-maker.
